newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Aleman rebounds in Nicaraguan election poll.
newsitem.headline: Aleman rebounds in Nicaraguan election poll.

text.p: Right-wing Nicaraguan presidential candidate Arnoldo Aleman rebounded in an election poll released on Friday, reversing a trend that had seen his lead dwindle heading into the Oct. 20 elections.

A Borge y Asociados poll gave Aleman of the Liberal Alliance coalition 41 percent of the vote, followed by former President Daniel Ortega of the left-wing Sandinista Front with 35 percent, and 21 other candidates a collective eight percent.

"Arnoldo Aleman, the Liberal Alliance candidate, would win the presidency in the first round of voting if the elections were held today," Victor Borge, president of Borge y Asociados S.A., told reporters.

If the 16 percent undecided voters are removed, Aleman received 48 percent of the vote and Ortega 41 percent, Borge said. Aleman needs 45 percent of the vote to win in the first round and avoid a run-off vote against Ortega.

The poll was a breath of fresh air for Aleman after a CID- Gallup poll last week gave him 34 percent support and Ortega 30 percent, showing his once seemingly insurmountable lead dwindling to four percentage points.
But the new poll also confirmed Ortega's upward surge, with his popularity soaring by 15 percent since last year and 10 percent since April.
Ortega headed the Sandinista government from 1979 to 1990, carrying out a massive socialist transformation of Nicaraguan society and fighting an eight-year civil war against U.S.-armed Contra rebels.
But he has emerged in 1996 as a moderate willing to work with the private sector and foreign investors.

His political rebirth is seen by analysts as a reflection of popular discontent with the economic crisis that has made Nicaragua the poorest country in Latin America after Haiti, according to a recent U.N. study.

Aleman, the former mayor of Managua, is a right-wing populist who has campaigned on an anti-Sandinista platform, promising to reverse many of the changes implemented by the former left-wing government.
The poll was carried out Sept. 1-6, and surveyed 1,200 Nicaraguans with an accuracy of plus or minus five percent.
